brief_extract:
The E.A.W. has early been responsive to the attractions of a new locality, and, like all housewives “settling in,” it has found the shops of special interest, whether they are the unique Liberty’s store, the nearest large neighbour, or the host of small Continental food stores and restaurants which abound in Soho. It was thought that readers would like to share in the practical results of a “browse” made by the Head of the Housecraft Department, and they can do this through the article “The World’s Your Oyster.”

The E.A.W., too, has shared the curiosity felt by all newcomers regarding those who were there before, and researches have produced some interesting information on the 17th century Major Foubert, who gave his name to the street.

brief_context: Place from which M. Foubert recently arrived in 1681.
brief_extract:
Some interesting old books have revealed some tit-bits of history, and among them an extract from John Evelyn's Diary for 17th September, 1681, records this:—
"I went with M. Foubert about taking ye Countesse of Bristol's house for an academie, he being lately come from Paris for his religion and resolving to settle here."
Major or Monsieur Foubert was a French refugee who established a Riding Academy to which Charles II gave £100 in 1681, for it was hoped that it would lessen the expense of sending children to France to be taught military exercises. Evelyn records a later visit to the Academy with Lord Cornwallis to see various scions of the nobility receiving equestrian instruction, and it is interesting to note that the Duke of Cumberland, the future victor of Culloden, received his first riding lesson here.

brief_context: Country where Miss Mitchell visited several kitchens and schools.
brief_extract: Of particular interest in bringing the electrical message to the villages was the Maison Heureuse, a portable show bungalow capable of seating about 70 people. Miss Mitchell visited a dozen or so large-scale kitchens in Belgium ranging from one in a monastery to one in a telephone exchange, she inspected the domestic science departments in several schools, and attended exhibitions and demonstrations of various kinds. Her Belgian hosts, conscious of their artistic heritage, ensured that she also visited a special art exhibition in Antwerp, and that she was shown the beauties of their ancient cities.

brief_context: Floodlit city visited by Miss Mitchell.
brief_extract:
As she observed, "Every visit was full of human and business interest. It was interesting to find how each district was able to put an entirely local interpretation upon the list of things I said I wished to see and study."

Luxembourg
A brief visit to Luxembourg revealed the beauties of a floodlit city, and provided the opportunity of seeing a festival procession from the Cathedral. As Miss Mitchell wrote, "the day was utterly perfect, with brilliant sun, blue sky, trees just beginning to turn colour, wonderful distant scenery and a fairy-story-book setting at hand." A visit to two old people's homes emphasised the national care for the welfare of the old in this tiny State.

brief_context: Area visited for its beauties during the tour.
brief_extract:
Talks with the wife and daughter of her host from the supply authority and with the Mother Superior of one of the homes provided Miss Mitchell with some typical Luxembourg recipes. Sandwiched in between special electrical studies was a flying visit to see the beauties of the Moselle Valley. Holland

The 30th Annual Conference of the E.A.W. to be held at Llandudno from 30th April to 3rd May, 1956, promises to equal if not surpass other out-of-London Conferences in the pleasure and interest to be provided. It will follow the well-tried pattern of an Opening Session, an Annual Luncheon, a Civic Reception and a Branches' Party, together with a variety of visits to suit all tastes.

brief_context: Compared to Pompeii in its deserted loveliness.
brief_extract:
As, how-
ever, we think of the populous
and traffic burdened streets of to-
day we may remind ourselves of
the position in the 18th and 19th
centuries. Mackay in his "Jour-
ney through England" in 1722
describes Great Marlborough
Street, as "surpassing anything
that is called a street in the mag-
nificence of its buildings and gar-
dens." and a 19th century writer
speaks of the deserted effects of
the fashionable world leaving
Town at the end of the Season—
"Regent Street assimilates to
Pompeii in its loveliness."
Perhaps we can end on a really
modern note, for the 200 years old
church of St. Giles-in-the-Fields
had a floodlighting system switch-
ed on on 10th November, 1955.

brief_context: Visited bungalow estate with communal laundry and studied kitchen refrigeration.
article_title: Kitchens and Communal Laundries in Europe
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE    APRIL, 1956

Continued from page 251
In Denmark she visited a new bungalow estate with a communal laundry, planned on the basis of the traditional once a month wash; a laundry in a municipally run old people's home, which also washed for four kindergartens; and communal laundries provided in blocks of flats. Miss Mitchell inspected a wide variety of kitchens to study the type of equipment and the kitchen lay-out in relation to the style of the national cooking.

brief_context: Observed typical cooking equipment such as chip fryers and boilers.
article_title: Kitchens and Communal Laundries in Europe
brief_extract:
Miss Mitchell inspected a wide variety of kitchens to study the type of equipment and the kitchen lay-out in relation to the style of the national cooking. In the Belgian kitchens, the outstanding features are a large and elaborate chip fryer; a mayonnaise machine; enormous soup boilers; a large coffee maker; and a sauteuse. One notices an absence of steaming ovens, of grills except a few bottom heat type and of large ovens except for patis-
serie.

brief_context: Studied regional differences in kitchen equipment and daily meal habits.
article_title: Kitchens and Communal Laundries in Europe
brief_extract: Sweets are not so important as in this country. Similar equipment is found in southern Holland, but further north chip pans diminish in size, Mayonnaise makers vanish and tea making apparatus and slicing machines appear. There is still not much use for ovens.

brief_context: Mentioned as having kitchen equipment similar to Belgium.
article_title: Kitchens and Communal Laundries in Europe
brief_extract: There is still not much use for ovens. Luxembourg is like Belgium, while in Denmark adequate refrigeration space is required. The actual cooking equipment differs little, but the steaming oven appears.

brief_context: Location of Dame Caroline Haslett's home.
article_title: Resignation of Dame Caroline Haslett, D.B.E., J.P.
brief_extract:
Illness has caused her
withdrawal from public life for
the past two years, but as hon-
orary adviser she will continue
with the Association which she
has directed since its inception 32
years ago. As Dame Caroline surveys the
scene from her Suffolk home she
will see a monument to her life
work in the homes of this country,
and especially in the lives of its
women. Her name will always
be associated with the develop-
ment of the domestic uses of elec-
tricity, bringing happier home-
making, and opportunities for
richer, fuller lives, with the reali-
sation of the potentialities of
women in a modern technical
world.

location_standardised: Crawley, West Sussex, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned in relation to the Crawley Development Corporation.
article_title: Resignation of Dame Caroline Haslett, D.B.E., J.P.
brief_extract:
She herself has been the first
and often the only woman to hold
many appointments in this
country, to be a member of official
delegations abroad, and to repre-
sent this country during and after
the war. To mention but a few of her
many outstanding offices, she
was appointed a member of the
newly created British Electricity
Authority in 1947, the first
woman chairman of the British
Electrical Development Associa-
tion, the only woman member of
the Council of the British Institute
of Management, and a member of
the Crawley Development Cor-
poration. Her understanding of precision
methods and of time and motion
study in the factory led her to
advocate the application of scien-
tific management in the home.

brief_context: Referencing hydro-electric power output levels.
brief_extract:
As electricity con-
sumption and productivity went
hand in hand, the Government
had embarked on the most ambi-
tious programme of any country
in the world, in constructing 12
nuclear power stations by 1965. The total output of hydro-
electric power in Great Britain
was only 2.6% of the total power
produced, a lower figure than in
countries with greater water sup-
plies, but there were seven impor-
tant hydro-electric stations in
North Wales. In addition to those
to be seen by the delegates, at
Maentwrog and Dolgarrog, inter-
esting projects were planned on
the Rheidol and at Festiniog; the
latter, a pumped storage scheme
with an intended generating capa-
city of 300,000 kW., would be the
first of its kind in the country.

article_title: VISIT TO CAMBRIAN UNITED DAIRIES PROCESSING DEPOT, MARSHFIELD
brief_extract:
M. HEARD, Magazine Secretary, Cardiff
The tour started at the intake platform where the churns are unloaded from lorries, inspected by a professional “sniffer,” and the milk poured into a huge vat, from which it travels by pipe to a room containing four 3,000 gallon tanks, brine-cooled to a temperature of 38-40°F. The milk is then taken to the pasteurising plant, where its temperature is now raised to the critical level of 160.5°F., maintained for 15 seconds, and again cooled to 38°F.

article_title: What is an adequate number of plug points ?
brief_extract: This is dangerous because its insulation quickly wears away and a short circuit can damage the carpet badly and even set the house on fire. This lack of plug points in British homes is one which has been enthusiastically tackled by the electrical industry both before and since the war. In the last few years particularly, considerable progress has been made towards the ideal of having an adequate number of plug points in the home, and already this is being achieved in hundreds of thousands of new houses now being built, and in old houses where the electrical installation is being brought up to date.

The National Register of Electrical Installation Contractors is an independent body directed by representatives of important Associations interested in electrical installation work, including
The Institution of Electrical Engineers, The Association of Consulting Engineers, The Electrical Contractors' Association of Scotland, The Electrical Association for Women. Electrical Installation Contractors holding the Certificate of the National Register have given evidence of competency; their work is subject to periodical inspection; they undertake to pay rates of wages and observe conditions of employment not less favourable than those of the appropriate trade agreement; and observe the Regulations for the Electrical Equipment of Buildings issued by the Institution of Electrical Engineers.

brief_extract:
Shrewsbury had a meeting at the
Radbrooke College of Domestic
Science, where the Principal (Branch
President) gave a talk on "Man-made
Fabrics—their Use and Care." A de-
monstration of rug making was pre-
ceded by an "electrical flash" regard-
ing electric blankets. A visit was paid
to Pitchford Hall, formerly the home
of the late Lady Sybil Grant and now
the property of the National Library
of Wales. It was interesting to see how
electric light and power had been in-
troduced without proving an ana-
chronism — gorgeous Georgian silver
candle sconces had been skilfully elec-
trified without any loss of beauty, and
concealed lighting enhanced the ap-
pearance of valuable old paintings.

brief_context: A mill visited where eiderdowns are produced.
brief_extract: The bedspreads are woven in 1,000 yard lengths, and each travels over rollers into a room where girls with a skilful slash divided it into separate bedspreads, which are trimmed, folded, hemmed and pressed. At the Victoria Mill a hundred or more eiderdowns are made every day. This mill employs 112 people.

brief_context: A mill visited where bedspreads are woven and designed.
brief_extract: Members also saw the blanket weaving department, and were informed that there are 3,676 threads in a 90-inch Blansheet. At the Saville Mill bedcovers of all kinds are woven, from the gay and gaudy cheaper bedspreads to the most expensive "Marcelle" so beloved of our grandmothers, and still the most hard-wearing. Many of these are specially woven for hospitals, shipping lines, etc.

brief_context: Mentioned in relation to the maple leaf design on bedspreads.
brief_extract: The pattern cards are arranged and fitted by men skilled in this trade of "jacquard harness fitting". It is fascinating to watch these looms at work and to see the design grow in the bedspread before one's eyes—lovely little cot covers with all nursery rhyme figures in pastel shades, larger covers with the maple leaf of Canada, and many other designs. Members saw bedspreads having fringe attached by a special machine, which forms the fringe as it works.

article_title: VISIT TO SOUTH WALES SWITCHGEAR LTD.
brief_extract: HEARD, Magazine Secretary, Cardiff Branch. The factory, situated in the Sirhowy Valley in Monmouth, is one of several which have brought industrial employment to South Wales. This particular works deals with the heavier types of electrical equipment and apparatus required by power generating stations for handling and controlling electricity through its various stages from the high voltage source down to the level at which it is delivered to our homes, also the massive equipment required to supply and control the enormous quantities of electrical power needed by industrial undertakings.
